Prevention: Apply banding materials like grease or tangle foot to prevent ants from climbing to the canopy to introduce the mealybugs.
Construct slippery bands of alkathene or plastic sheets around the tree trunk at about one meter above the ground level.
Use clean planting materials from certified nurseries such as
KALRO Mutuga, JKUAT to reduce spread of infestation into new fields.
Conserve natural enemies; lacewings, pirate bugs, lady beetles and parasitoids by maintaining natural habitat.
Avoid the use of infested plant materials.
Before planting, seedlings can be treated by immersing them in heated water (mix equal volumes of boiling and cold water) for 5 to 10 minutes to kill the pest.
Plant early in the rainy season to allow citrus to grow well, before the dry season, as strong plants are more likely to withstand pest attack.
Use soil amendments and mulch to avoid moisture stress in sandy or poor soils.
Mealybug numbers are higher in poor soil, and may cause damage in spite of the presence of natural enemies.
Restrict movement of infested planting materials across to mealybug-free areas.
Monitoring: Inspect regularly for dark sticky covering on affected part (sooty mold).
Check for ants climbing to the plant canopy.
Check for white immobile oval and flattened insects with body covered with a white mealy powder on the leaves, stems, fruit stalks and growing tips.
Symptoms on the plant include stunting, wilting, leaf distortion, leaf fall, rosetting of the stem, bunchy top and dieback.
Ants may also be present as they protect the mealybugs from natural enemies and feed on the honeydew they produce.
Black sooty mould may grow on the leaves and stem in the presence of honeydew.
Take action when you notice white waxy material on shoot tips, leaves and stems or any signs of mealybugs.
Direct Control: Prune and burn the highly infested plant parts.
Spray the affected plant part with a mild solution of water with dish washing detergent at rate of 1 tea spoonful of detergent in 1 litre of water.
